stories.headline: A reasoning model that runs on a laptop
stories.deck: Quantised weights put frontier-class inference on consumer hardware, and the local-first crowd has opinions.
body: The release landed without a livestream, which is itself part of the story. Benchmarks put the model within a rounding error of systems that needed a datacentre eighteen months ago, and the weights are small enough to sit comfortably on an external drive.

What changed is not the architecture but the quantisation pipeline. By holding attention layers at higher precision while aggressively compressing the feed-forward blocks, the team kept reasoning performance largely intact at roughly a quarter of the memory footprint.

The practical consequence is that a mid-range laptop from the last three years can now run the kind of multi-step reasoning that previously meant an API call and a per-token bill. Early community benchmarks are noisy and should be treated with caution, but the direction is not in dispute.

stories.headline: EU timeline for model audits slips to 2027
stories.deck: Compliance teams get another year; the people who built the auditing tooling get a harder conversation with their investors.
body: The delay was framed as a technical consultation extension rather than a retreat, but the effect is the same: mandatory third-party audits for general-purpose models will not bind until well into 2027.

Industry groups had argued that the audit methodology was underspecified and that firms could not meaningfully prepare against a moving target. Civil society groups countered that the specification had been stable for months and the objection was really about cost.
For anyone building compliance tooling, the runway just got longer and the urgency just got smaller — a mixed result that markets tend to price as bad news.

stories.headline: A quieter attention variant halves memory at long context
stories.deck: No press release, no demo, just a preprint and a benchmark table that is difficult to argue with.
body: The paper proposes a sparsity pattern that is learned rather than fixed, letting the model decide which earlier tokens deserve full attention and which can be summarised into a compressed cache.

Memory use at 200k context drops by roughly half against a dense baseline, with perplexity degradation the authors describe as within noise. The result has not been independently reproduced at scale, which is the usual and correct caveat.

What makes this interesting is less the number than the framing: long context has been treated as a hardware problem for two years, and this is a reminder that it is still partly an algorithms problem.

stories.headline: Agent frameworks consolidate around one protocol
stories.deck: Three competing tool-calling standards became one this week, largely because customers refused to integrate three.
body: Standardisation in this space has been predicted for two years and repeatedly failed to arrive, mostly because each vendor's protocol was load-bearing for its own product.

The forcing function was procurement. Enterprise buyers started writing protocol-agnostic requirements into contracts, and maintaining a bespoke integration surface stopped being a moat and started being a line item.
Migration guides are already out. The interesting question is what happens to the smaller frameworks whose main differentiator was the integration layer they are now giving up.

stories.headline: Inference prices fall again across three providers
stories.deck: The third round of cuts this year, and the first where the cheapest tier is genuinely usable for production work.
body: Price cuts at this cadence stop being news and start being a trend line. What is notable this round is that the reductions landed on the mid-tier models rather than the smallest ones.
That matters because mid-tier is where most production traffic actually sits. Cutting the price of a model nobody ships is marketing; cutting the price of the workhorse is margin.
Analysts expect the compression to continue through the year as capacity comes online faster than demand for the largest models.

stories.headline: A widely cited eval harness fails reproduction
stories.deck: Two independent groups could not match the published numbers. The maintainers say the config defaults changed.
body: The discrepancy traces to a default sampling temperature that shifted between minor versions, which is a small change with outsized consequences for a benchmark used in dozens of papers.
Nobody is alleging bad faith. The failure mode is mundane: a configuration surface that was never treated as a stable API being depended on as though it were one.
The maintainers have pinned defaults and cut a new release. The papers citing the old numbers remain as they are.

stories.headline: A major open-weights licence quietly adds a usage cap
stories.deck: Still free for almost everyone, but the definition of 'almost' now has a number attached to it.
body: The revised terms introduce a monthly active user threshold above which commercial use requires a negotiated licence. Below it, nothing changes.
The threshold is high enough that the overwhelming majority of users will never encounter it, which is precisely the design. It is a competitor clause dressed as a fairness clause.
Whether this still counts as open source is a question the licence-steward community has been arguing about for long enough that the answer is probably 'it depends who is asking'.

stories.headline: Two datacentre projects stall on grid connection
stories.deck: The bottleneck for frontier training is increasingly a substation, not a chip.
body: Both projects had secured hardware allocations and planning permission. Neither could secure a grid connection date inside the decade.
This is becoming the defining constraint of the buildout. Compute can be manufactured on a two-year horizon; transmission infrastructure cannot.
Several operators have responded by siting new capacity next to existing generation rather than near demand, which solves the power problem and creates a latency one.

stories.headline: A distillation recipe nobody else picked up
stories.deck: Eleven upvotes and one comment, but the method is clean and the ablations are honest.
body: Buried under the week's louder releases, this preprint describes a staged distillation approach that trades a small amount of accuracy for a large reduction in student training cost.
The ablation table is the good part. The authors report the configurations that did not work, including two that look obviously promising and are not.
Included here because a digest that only surfaces what everyone already saw is a worse digest.
